prompt: Cultural competence includes:

options.text: Applying a cultural guide's beliefs to every client of that group
Using a bilingual family member as the interpreter to build trust
Asking about health beliefs/preferences rather than stereotyping
Treating every client identically so no one is singled out

explanation: Assess individuals; use qualified interpreters.

distractorExplanations.a: Assuming everyone in a group holds the same beliefs is stereotyping; each client is assessed individually.
distractorExplanations.b: Family interpreters compromise accuracy and confidentiality; qualified medical interpreters are used.
distractorExplanations.d: Identical care ignores individual beliefs and preferences; cultural competence adapts care to the person.

prompt: Milieu therapy refers to:

options.text: Using rewards and tokens to reinforce desired behaviors on the unit
Individual sessions exploring unconscious conflicts
Gradual exposure to feared situations in a safe setting
Using the therapeutic environment and structured interactions

explanation: Psychiatric nursing uses milieu as a treatment tool. The aim is to support recovery.

distractorExplanations.a: Rewards and tokens describe behavior modification (token economy), not milieu therapy.
distractorExplanations.b: Exploring unconscious conflicts is psychodynamic psychotherapy, not use of the therapeutic environment.
distractorExplanations.c: Graduated exposure to feared situations is systematic desensitization used for phobias.

prompt: When a client is angry and pacing, an appropriate initial approach is?

options.text: Maintain safe distance, calm tone, offer to listen, and ensure exit access for staff
Cornering the client in a small room alone
Matching anger with yelling
Touching suddenly from behind

explanation: De-escalation prioritizes safety and respect.

distractorExplanations.b: Don’t trap.
distractorExplanations.c: Stay calm.
distractorExplanations.d: Avoid startling touch.

prompt: A client facing limb amputation expresses body image disturbance. The nurse should

options.text: Reassure the client that a prosthesis will make life the same as before
Encourage expression of feelings and involve rehab/support resources
Delay viewing the site until the client is discharged home
Focus teaching on stump care and defer feelings to the psychologist

explanation: Body image work is legitimate psychosocial care.

distractorExplanations.a: Promising life will be the same is false reassurance that brushes aside the client's grief over body change.
distractorExplanations.c: Gradual viewing of the site with support helps adjustment; delaying it until discharge worsens body image issues.
distractorExplanations.d: Body image concerns are part of nursing care; the nurse encourages expression rather than deferring it.

prompt: Confidentiality in mental health settings means:

options.text: Protect PHI, with no exceptions even when harm to others is threatened
Share PHI freely with the client's family since they are caregivers
Protect PHI while explaining limits (harm to self/others, abuse reporting)
Protect PHI, but disclose any details the client's employer requests

explanation: Tarasoff-type duties and mandated reporting create limits to confidentiality.

distractorExplanations.a: Duty-to-warn/protect and mandated abuse reporting are legal exceptions to confidentiality.
distractorExplanations.b: Family members need the client's authorization to receive PHI, even when they are caregivers.
distractorExplanations.d: Employers have no right to PHI without the client's authorization.

prompt: A client with heart failure has 2+ pitting edema and crackles. Priority nursing action is often to:

options.text: Elevate HOB, monitor SpO2/respiratory status, and report changes
Place flat with legs elevated to reduce edema, and recheck in 4 hours
Encourage oral fluids to thin secretions and monitor lung sounds
Hold daily weights and I&O until the crackles resolve

explanation: Fluid overload threatens gas exchange; follow ABC and orders. Administer ordered diuretics/O2 per plan.

distractorExplanations.b: Lying flat with legs up increases venous return and worsens pulmonary congestion; the HOB is raised.
distractorExplanations.c: Extra fluid worsens overload in heart failure; fluids are usually restricted, not encouraged.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily weights and I&O are key to tracking fluid status and continue during overload.

prompt: Hypoglycemia in a conscious client who can swallow is treated with:

options.text: Glucagon 1 mg IM, then a complex-carbohydrate snack
15 g rapid-acting carbohydrate, recheck per protocol
Protein snack such as peanut butter, then recheck in 1 hour
A full meal with protein, then recheck at the next scheduled time

explanation: Treat low glucose first; unresponsive clients need emergency glucagon/IV dextrose per protocol/RN-provider. This is the 15-15 rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Glucagon is for clients who cannot swallow or are unresponsive; a conscious client takes oral fast carbohydrate.
distractorExplanations.c: Protein and fat slow glucose absorption; fast carbohydrate is given first, with a recheck in 15 minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: A full meal acts too slowly and the recheck is needed in about 15 minutes, not at the next scheduled check.

prompt: A client on warfarin should be taught to:

options.text: Avoid all vitamin K foods and report bleeding; keep INR appointments
Keep vitamin K consistent and use ibuprofen rather than acetaminophen
Keep vitamin K intake consistent and report bleeding/bruising
Keep vitamin K consistent and double the next dose if one is missed

explanation: Anticoagulation teaching focuses on consistency, bleeding signs, and interaction awareness. Keep INR appointments.

distractorExplanations.a: Vitamin K intake should be consistent, not eliminated; avoiding it makes INR unstable.
distractorExplanations.b: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen raise bleeding risk with warfarin; acetaminophen is preferred for minor pain.
distractorExplanations.d: Missed warfarin doses are not doubled; clients take the missed dose the same day or follow provider instructions.

prompt: Post-op client with PCA morphine is difficult to arouse with RR 6/min. Priority action

options.text: Lower the PCA basal rate, recheck vital signs in 30 minutes, and report at shift end
Let the client sleep since pain is controlled, and recheck RR in 1 hour
Teach the family to press the PCA button when the client grimaces
Stop the PCA/opioids, support airway/breathing, stimulate, and notify RN/provider

explanation: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is an emergency. Prepare naloxone as ordered.

distractorExplanations.a: RR 6 with poor arousal is an emergency; the opioid is stopped and help called now, not reported at shift end.
distractorExplanations.b: Difficulty arousing with RR 6 is opioid-induced respiratory depression, not restful sleep, and needs action now.
distractorExplanations.c: PCA by proxy is unsafe; only the client presses the button, so sedation limits further dosing.

prompt: Signs of wound infection include

options.text: Increasing redness, warmth, purulent drainage, odor, fever
Approximated edges with scant serous drainage on day 1 only as definitive infection
Normal pruritus of healing without other signs as infection proof
Absent drainage and afebrile state as infection

explanation: Differentiate normal inflammatory healing from infection; report changes.

distractorExplanations.b: Early scant serous can be expected.
distractorExplanations.c: Itch alone isn’t infection.
distractorExplanations.d: Those suggest no infection.

prompt: A client with COPD should be taught pursed-lip breathing to:

options.text: Increase inspiratory volume and strengthen the diaphragm
Prolong exhalation and prevent airway collapse/air trapping
Raise CO2 levels to stimulate the respiratory drive
Shorten exhalation so more oxygen is inhaled per minute

explanation: Pursed-lip breathing improves ventilation patterns in COPD.

distractorExplanations.a: Strengthening the diaphragm is the goal of diaphragmatic breathing; pursed-lip breathing prolongs exhalation.
distractorExplanations.c: Pursed-lip breathing helps empty trapped air and lower CO2 retention; it does not aim to raise CO2.
distractorExplanations.d: Pursed-lip breathing lengthens exhalation to prevent air trapping; shortening it worsens hyperinflation.

prompt: Potassium chloride IV should never be

options.text: Given as a diluted infusion per policy when ordered
Monitored with labs when replacement is underway
Given as an IV push/bolus
Held when hyperkalemia is present per order

explanation: IVP KCl can cause fatal dysrhythmias; infusions use pumps/dilution rules.

distractorExplanations.a: Controlled infusion is the route.
distractorExplanations.b: Labs guide therapy.
distractorExplanations.d: Hold if high K+.

prompt: For a client with a cast, report immediately

options.text: Mild itching under the cast without neurovascular change
Warm, pink toes with brisk capillary refill and mild swelling
Dull ache relieved by elevation and the ordered analgesic
Increasing pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, paralysis

explanation: Compartment syndrome is limb-threatening—escalate ASAP. These are compartment syndrome signs.

distractorExplanations.a: Mild itch can occur.
distractorExplanations.b: Warm, pink toes with brisk refill show adequate perfusion; mild swelling is managed with elevation.
distractorExplanations.c: Pain relieved by elevation and analgesics is expected; compartment syndrome pain is unrelieved and increasing.

prompt: NG tube placement verification before feeding is best confirmed by:

options.text: Facility-required method (often x-ray initially; pH/markings per policy)
Air bolus auscultation over the epigastrium as the sole check
Observing for bubbling when the tube end is placed in a cup of water
Confirming the client can talk clearly and is not coughing after insertion

explanation: Misplacement risks aspiration; follow current verification standards. Air auscultation alone is not acceptable.

distractorExplanations.b: Auscultating an air bolus is unreliable and cannot tell gastric from respiratory placement.
distractorExplanations.c: Bubbling in water is an outdated, unreliable test that can mislead in either direction.
distractorExplanations.d: Small-bore tubes can enter the airway with no coughing or voice change, so absence of symptoms proves nothing.

prompt: A client with dehydration may show

options.text: Bradycardia, moist mucous membranes, and pale dilute urine output
Tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, concentrated urine
Jugular venous distention, weight gain, and peripheral edema
Tachycardia, dry mucous membranes, and dilute high-volume urine

explanation: Volume depletion signs guide fluid resuscitation orders and monitoring.

distractorExplanations.a: Dehydration causes tachycardia, dry membranes, and concentrated urine; these findings suggest normal or excess volume.
distractorExplanations.c: JVD, weight gain, and edema are signs of fluid overload, the opposite of dehydration.
distractorExplanations.d: In dehydration the kidneys conserve water, so urine is concentrated and low in volume, not dilute.

prompt: Insulin lispro (rapid-acting) should generally be given

options.text: Thirty to sixty minutes before meals like regular insulin
At bedtime with a snack to cover overnight glucose levels
At mealtime / when the tray is present per timing rules
Once daily at the same time each morning like insulin glargine

explanation: Match rapid insulin to carbohydrate intake to prevent hypoglycemia. Onset is about 15 minutes.

distractorExplanations.a: Giving lispro 30–60 minutes early follows regular insulin timing and risks hypoglycemia before the meal.
distractorExplanations.b: Overnight coverage comes from basal insulin; rapid-acting lispro at bedtime risks nocturnal hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.d: Once-daily dosing describes basal insulin such as glargine, not rapid-acting mealtime lispro.

prompt: Early hypoxia sign often includes:

options.text: Cyanosis of the lips and nail beds
Bradycardia and hypotension
Decreased LOC and bradypnea
Restlessness and tachycardia

explanation: Late signs include cyanosis; act on early mental status/VS changes.

distractorExplanations.a: Cyanosis is a late sign of hypoxia; earlier signs are restlessness and tachycardia.
distractorExplanations.b: Bradycardia and hypotension appear late as hypoxia worsens; early on the heart rate rises.
distractorExplanations.c: Decreasing LOC and slowed breathing are late, ominous signs; early hypoxia causes restlessness and tachypnea.

prompt: A client receiving a blood transfusion develops chills, fever, and back pain. The nurse should

options.text: Stop the transfusion, keep IV line open with NS, and notify provider
Slow the transfusion rate, give acetaminophen, and recheck in 15 minutes
Stop the transfusion, flush the blood tubing with D5W, and notify provider
Finish the unit quickly, then report the symptoms to the provider

explanation: Suspect acute hemolytic/febrile reaction—stop blood, maintain access, escalate. Follow transfusion reaction steps per protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Chills, fever, and back pain may be a hemolytic reaction; the transfusion is stopped, not slowed.
distractorExplanations.c: D5W hemolyzes red cells; the line is kept open with normal saline through new tubing.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuing the transfusion gives more incompatible blood; the reaction requires stopping it immediately.

prompt: Left-sided weakness after stroke: nursing care includes:

options.text: Reposition the client by pulling on the weak arm, which has less pain sensation
Approach from the intact side and protect the weak side
Place food on the left side of the mouth and offer thin liquids
Hold the cane in the hand on the weak side and advance the strong leg first

explanation: Safety and rehab principles guide hemiparesis care; dysphagia screens matter. Use assistive devices per the PT plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling on a weak arm can cause shoulder subluxation; reduced sensation increases injury risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Food goes on the unaffected (right) side, and thin liquids raise aspiration risk with dysphagia.
distractorExplanations.d: The cane is held on the strong side and advanced with the weak leg for support.

prompt: Digitalis toxicity warning signs to report include

options.text: Fine hand tremor, polyuria, and a persistent metallic taste in the mouth
Tinnitus, hearing loss, and rising serum creatinine
Anorexia, nausea, visual changes (halos), and bradycardia/dysrhythmias
Hyperactivity with tachycardia and flushing as the classic toxicity pattern

explanation: Narrow therapeutic index—monitor apical pulse and labs (K+, dig level) per orders.

distractorExplanations.a: Fine tremor, polyuria, and metallic taste are typical lithium side effects, not digoxin toxicity.
distractorExplanations.b: Tinnitus and rising creatinine suggest ototoxic/nephrotoxic drugs like aminoglycosides or vancomycin.
distractorExplanations.d: Digoxin toxicity typically causes bradycardia and dysrhythmias with GI and visual symptoms, not hyperactivity.
